title: Walking Tour
description: Put four names on the map of the British Isles and stop mixing an island up with a state: the British Isles are a group of islands, Great Britain is the island that holds England, Scotland and Wales, Ireland is the other main island, and the United Kingdom is the country that adds Northern Ireland to those three — so Northern Ireland is in the UK without being on Great Britain, and the Republic of Ireland is in the British Isles without being in the UK, with London, Edinburgh, Cardiff, Belfast and Dublin each in its place and the Atlantic to the west, the North Sea to the east and the English Channel to the south. Then describe a country with the model in three moves (the whole it belongs to, where it sits inside it, its neighbours and on which side), with border, constituent, cosmopolitan, venue, year round, official residence, former and spectacular, and the words of praise that are not interchangeable (captivating, breathtaking, magnificent, splendid, to revive). Read a walking-tour ad as five answers — what, when, where do I turn up, how long, how much — then read it again for what it does not print, because an ad proves only what it prints. Tell describing from persuading and from giving an opinion, and a text written to inform from one written to persuade or to narrate. Build the superlative the length of the adjective calls for (the oldest, the warmest, the busiest, the most captivating, the most memorable) with its spelling rules and its irregulars, and weigh what it really claims: the largest, the second largest, one of the most spectacular. Hear the long vowels of walk, first and guard against the short one of odd, never say work for walk, and voice the th when north becomes northern. Finally, take the microphone and plan a two-hour guided tour of your own town
